Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a debt collector's letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**A collection letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could reasonably read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.**

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bars a debt collector from using "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt." 15 U.S.C. § 1692e. The Act is a remedial consumer-protection statute. This Court therefore evaluates collection letters from the perspective of the "least sophisticated debtor." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000); *Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453–54 (3d Cir. 2006). That standard protects "the gullible as well as the shrewd," and it is lower than the standard of a reasonable debtor. *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 221 (3d Cir. 2008); *Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 148 (3d Cir. 2013). It is not a standard that lets collectors escape liability by pointing to the one reading of a letter that happens to be accurate.

**A. A letter that supports an inaccurate reading is deceptive.**

This Court has long held that a collection letter is deceptive "when it can be reasonably read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 222 (quoting *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455); *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. The test asks only whether the inaccurate reading is reasonable. It does not ask whether it is the most natural reading, or whether the collector intended it. *See Brown*, 464 F.3d at 454–55. Nor does it matter that a more careful reader might have worked out the accurate meaning. The standard presumes a debtor with only "a quite low level of sophistication," who reads with "some care" but is not a careful, legally trained reader. *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298–99 (3d Cir. 2008); *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221.

The ambiguity rule follows from the statute's purpose. A collector controls the wording of its letter. If it chooses language that admits an inaccurate reading, the debtor should not bear the risk. A debtor who reads the inaccurate meaning may pay a debt, or an amount, that the debtor does not owe. Or the debtor may forgo rights the Act protects. Section 1692e does not make a collector's liability depend on the debtor's skill at resolving ambiguity. *See Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997–98 (3d Cir. 2011) (applying the least-sophisticated-debtor standard and focusing on the letter's text and its overall impression on that debtor).

**B. The inquiry is objective, and the collector's intent is irrelevant.**

Whether a letter is deceptive is judged objectively by how the letter would be understood. A plaintiff need not show that the collector meant to mislead. *See Brown*, 464 F.3d at 454; *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 417–19 (3d Cir. 2015). Nor does the plaintiff need to show that she herself was actually confused. The question is whether the letter *could* mislead the least sophisticated debtor. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55; *Caprio*, 709 F.3d at 148–49. The rule is also limited. It requires that the inaccurate reading be reasonable, not "bizarre or idiosyncratic." It also requires that the misleading statement be material, meaning that it could affect the least sophisticated debtor's decisions about the debt. *See Jensen*, 791 F.3d at 419–21; *Campuzano-Burgos*, 550 F.3d at 299. Those limits do not protect a letter that, by its own wording, invites a reading that misstates the debt, the debtor's options, or the debtor's rights.

**C. Application.**

[Plaintiff's letter] contains the language "[quote operative language]." One reasonable reading is that [accurate meaning]. A second reasonable reading, which the least sophisticated debtor could easily adopt, is that [inaccurate meaning]. That second reading is false because [explain]. The inaccuracy is also material. It bears on [whether and how much to pay / whether to dispute the debt / the debtor's rights], and so it could affect the debtor's decisions about the debt. *See Jensen*, 791 F.3d at 419–21. Under *Wilson*, *Brown*, and *Rosenau*, the existence of an accurate alternative reading does not save the letter. Because the letter can reasonably be read in two ways and one is inaccurate, Defendant violated § 1692e.

**D. Conclusion.**

This Court should hold that Defendant's letter violated 15 U.S.C. § 1692e. The least sophisticated debtor could reasonably read it to carry a materially inaccurate meaning, and that is enough.
